briefOverview: David honors his covenant with Jonathan by seeking out and showing generous kindness to Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth, restoring his inheritance and granting him a permanent place at the royal table.
summary: David inquires whether any descendants of Saul remain to whom he can show “the kindness of God,” for Jonathan’s sake. Ziba, a former servant of Saul, reports that Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth, who is lame in both feet, lives in Lo-debar. David summons Mephibosheth, reassures him not to fear, restores to him all the land that belonged to Saul, and decrees that he will always eat at the king’s table. David appoints Ziba with his sons and servants to farm the land for Mephibosheth’s household needs. Mephibosheth, expressing deep humility, settles in Jerusalem and continually eats at David’s table; he also has a young son named Micha.
externalContext: In the ancient Near East, new dynasties often eliminated or marginalized members of the prior royal house to secure the throne, so David’s proactive kindness to Saul’s line is notable. The term translated “kindness” (Hebrew hesed) often denotes covenant loyalty and steadfast love, aligning with David’s earlier commitments to Jonathan. Mephibosheth’s disability is previously explained in 2 Samuel 4:4, where a childhood accident left him lame. “Eating at the king’s table” signified high favor and ongoing provision, akin to being counted among the royal household. Ziba appears as a substantial household manager with many sons and servants, indicating the scale of administration attached to Saul’s former estate.
externalReferences: David’s action fulfills his covenant with Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:14–17), where he swore to show steadfast love to Jonathan’s house. It also aligns with David’s oath to Saul not to cut off Saul’s descendants (1 Samuel 24:21–22). Mephibosheth’s lameness has earlier narrative background in 2 Samuel 4:4. Later episodes revisit Ziba and Mephibosheth’s relationship and test perceptions of loyalty (2 Samuel 16:1–4; 2 Samuel 19:24–30).
practicalQuestions: What commitments have I made that I can honor with concrete kindness, even when I no longer “need” to?
How can I use authority or resources to restore others rather than to secure my own advantage?
Who today might feel like an outsider, and what would it look like to bring them to the “table” of belonging and provision?
Where can I practice covenantal faithfulness that mirrors God’s steadfast kindness?
How might I ensure that benevolence includes practical structures of support, not merely words (as David assigns Ziba’s household to serve Mephibosheth)?
uncertainAreas: “Kindness of God” may mean either kindness reflective of God’s character or kindness promised under oath before God; the text does not specify. Calling Mephibosheth “as one of the king’s sons” implies adoptive status, but no formal adoption formula is given. The precise location of Lo-debar and the full extent of Saul’s lands are not detailed here. Ziba’s motives and long-term faithfulness are not assessed in this chapter.
